World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Trusts are a 'breakfast buffet' for reducing tax. Is that about to change?
World.content:
Trusts give wealthy families and business owners a "breakfast buffet" of options to reduce their taxes, but changing the rules is complicated and may not raise much money, economists have warned.

Tuesday's federal budget is set to include changes to trust taxation alongside negative gearing and capital gains tax reform, according to several government sources, marking a partial return to Labor's failed 2019 tax policy agenda.

Trusts are a legal way for families to structure their financial affairs, offering more flexibility and control than alternatives and also providing lucrative opportunities to pay less tax.

There are nearly one million in Australia, many of them linked to small businesses.

CGT, negative gearing and trust taxes to change The government is still finalising the details of its budget, but several sources say three tax policies that featured in Labor's 2019 election campaign will be revived and rethought.

Labor's plans are unclear, but its previous policy was a 30 per cent minimum tax on funds distributed from trusts to their beneficiaries, to crack down on the ability to split income among family members and claim the tax-free threshold multiple times.

Kristen Sobeck, an economist at the University of Canberra, said the tax rules for trusts led to unfair outcomes and there was a strong case for reform.

"I call trusts a tax breakfast buffet or dessert bar, because they open up a range of options to choose from across the personal income tax system and the company tax system," she told the ABC.

"It leads to a situation where two people with the same income can have vastly different tax outcomes because one uses a trust and one does not."

How families use trusts

A trust has assets placed inside of it, such as businesses or properties, managed by a trustee who can distribute the proceeds to the beneficiaries of the trust, who are often members of the same family.

Trusts are a popular way for a trustee to exert control over their estate, including by specifying what happens to their wealth after they die. They can also protect the owners of a company from personal liability if the company is sued.

Trusts are either fixed or discretionary. In a fixed trust, income is distributed in consistent proportions, for instance, a 50-50 split between a married couple in business together. Discretionary trusts offer much more flexibility, opening avenues for tax planning.

"People create discretionary trusts so they can direct the income to whoever they choose," ANU economist Bob Breuning, a former Treasury official, told the ABC.

"If you're someone who earns a lot of income and you pay the top marginal tax rate of 47 per cent and you have someone you can split that income with who is paying zero tax, you can pay zero tax on that income," he said.

This practice, called income splitting, is one basic way for family members to share income so as to reduce taxes. Often, the family's earners will operate as sole traders, earn their money as business income, and distribute it among the family as "dividends".

More complicated structures involving holding companies and rules that allow people to move income around between different tax years can allow people to save hundreds of thousands of dollars, in what some economists call "a washing machine".

"A family with a trust can take advantage of everyone's tax-free threshold today, and whatever income they're not ready to use they get to plonk in a company which is also a beneficiary of the trust," Dr Sobeck said.

"That gets taxed at the company tax rate and stays there until they're ready to pay themselves, say in retirement, when the company tax is refunded, and they pay income tax at a lower rate."

Challenges for reform

The 30 per cent minimum tax Labor proposed in 2019 would reduce the benefits from income splitting. An expanded proposal from tax law professor Miranda Stewart would also tax undistributed income that is generated inside a trust.

In her recent tax paper, independent MP Allegra Spender argued this would simply push people to a different structure, instead making their family members shareholders of a private company and continuing to earn money as business income to pay less tax.

Negative gearing, CGT and trusts explained The government is poised to make changes to negative gearing, the capital gains tax discount and the tax treatment of trusts. So how do they work, and what could changes look like?

Instead, she proposed a 27.5 per cent tax on all investment income, regardless of whether it is earned through trusts or elsewhere.

Dr Sobeck said a 30 per cent flat tax could discourage people from using more complicated company structures within trusts, since they would rather pay the 25 per cent tax rate for small businesses.

"It would mean that people who are using these structures purely for the purpose of minimising tax and parking their income in this small company aren't going to be able to do that any more," she said.

Professor Breunig said any rate between 25 per cent and 30 per cent would be "reasonable" but warned trusts were "extremely complicated" and the number of people benefiting from trusts may not be as large as expected.

"It's easy to come up with scenarios where people could save a massive amount of tax, but the scope of the problem is difficult to determine, and it looks like people aren't taking maximum advantage," he said.

"To make trusts work, you have to be patient, and you have to have family members to distribute the money to, and a lot of people don't have those two things. A lot of people who use trusts probably don't get as much advantage as they would expect."

Dr Sobeck agreed there was significant uncertainty about how much money could be raised, especially since people may pursue other options to reduce their taxes.

"There would be some revenue gains, but how big it would be hard to say."

World.title: Trump wanted an American pope but not this American pope
World.content:
Popes, presidents and plots. Melodramatic, for sure, but a year into the papacy of Leo XIV, we know a lot about the jostling for power during the conclave of 2025. We also know why so much was at stake during those two days last May.

Foreign leaders and lobbyists thought they would write the next chapter in Catholic history. They failed and Leo is proving to be the pope some of them feared.

A new book, The Election of Pope Leo XIV: The Last Surprise of Pope Francis, by veteran Vatican reporters Gerard O'Connell and Elisabetta Pique, reveals it was not only Donald Trump who tried to get his way with the cardinals, although he was the most obvious.

The recently ousted prime minister of Hungary, Viktor Orban, used his ambassador to the Holy See, Eduard Habsburg, to press the case for the cardinal from Budapest, Peter Erdo, a strong Orban ally.

On the liberal side, French President Emmanuel Macron, in Rome for Francis's funeral, entertained cardinals to advocate for Jean-Marc Aveline, the popular Archbishop of Marseille, who shared his Europhile worldview.

Despite Donald Trump, Pope Leo has also been rebuilding relations with American Catholics of all stripes. (Reuters: Adam Gray)

The Napa Institute, an organisation of American free-market Catholics, spent lavishly in Rome leading up to the conclave, duchessing as many officials as it could to ensure the next pope would be nothing like Francis. He had criticised extreme capitalism and the fossil fuel industry. Their preference appeared to be retired New York Cardinal Timothy Dolan, who, just coincidentally, also happened to be the favourite of Trump.

Trump certainly wanted an American and he got it — just not the sort he was banking on.

'Louis is all MAGA'

In a now-infamous social media post on April 13, he called the pope "WEAK on crime, terrible on foreign policy". He said he preferred Leo's brother Louis "much better than I like him, because Louis is all MAGA. He gets it, and Leo doesn't!".

Tellingly, Trump said he "doesn't want a pope who criticises the president" and claimed the church only chose Leo because he was an American who could deal with the White House. It's possible Trump is right. But not in the way he thinks.

Just reflect on the first three months of last year. Trump was creating upheaval in the world, fracturing traditional alliances, plunging millions into need with his cuts to foreign aid, and hundreds of millions more into economic uncertainty with his tariff war. The full force of his round-up of irregular immigrants in the United States was yet to come but his intentions were clear. And his threats of force against foreign countries — including long-time allies Canada and Denmark — portended the sort of world that Pope Francis had feared.

In a now infamous social media post, on April 13, Donald Trump called the pope "WEAK on crime, terrible on foreign policy". (Reuters: Nathan Howard)

By the time of his death, Francis had appointed about 80 per cent of the cardinals who would choose his successor. They shared his vision of a church for the poor and, with the ghost of Francis looming over the conclave, the cardinals decided to project a very different American voice around the world.

What have we got with Pope Leo XIV? Born Robert Francis Prevost, he is a son of Chicago, the archetypal great American city characterised by its ethnic, religious, and working-class neighbourhoods.

He also spent much of his life outside the US, including 20 years as a missionary priest and then bishop in Peru. As a pastor, he has what Francis called "the smell of the sheep" about him.

Leo dealt with the effects of two civil wars: one inside the church between priests embracing liberation theology and lay groups embracing fundamentalism; the other in Peru between the Marxist guerillas of Shining Path and supporters of the right-wing government. He has faced and overcome conflict.

Uncompromising when the occasion demands

When Leo was elected, the consensus was that he would be like Francis to the core on economic justice, the environment, inter-religious understanding and world peace. He would preserve the church's teaching on the sanctity of life, from conception to natural death, and on sex, sexuality, surrogacy and gender, while extending mercy and pastoral care to all. In the language of politics, he would be like most popes of the past 150 years — centre-left on economics, environment and peace, and conservative on culture. And so it has proven to be.

But Leo would break with Francis's style and disposition, less inclined to the dramatic gesture, such as washing the feet of juvenile offenders on Maundy Thursday, and less spontaneous in his public comments. But when the occasion demands, Leo's language is as uncompromising as his predecessor's.

Why Trump turned on the pope US President Donald Trump described Pope Leo XIV's accession to the papacy as a meaningful moment for America. But now he has said the pontiff is hurting the Catholic Church, and is weak. Here's how their relationship has developed over the past year.

Francis spoke about "an economy that kills". Leo has been equally blunt but with a touch of poetry. "Woe to those who manipulate religion and the very name of God for their own military, economic and political gain, dragging that which is sacred into darkness and filth," he said during his recent trip to Africa.

It was a clear rebuke of Trump's Defence Secretary, Pete Hegseth, who claims the war on Iran is a divine mission.

Leo does not seek a fight with Trump, or any leader, but he is showing he will not resile from one, either. Too much is at stake.

After denouncing the Iran war — just as John Paul II had denounced the 2003 Iraq war — the president accused him of consorting with left-wing "losers" and indulging a nuclear-armed theocracy. But Leo was defiant. "I'm not afraid of the Trump administration or speaking out loudly of the message of the gospel," he said.

A year on from his election, our first impressions of Pope Leo XIV remain the most lasting and revealing. (Reuters: Remo Casilli)

Events have forced Leo to confront the world that Trump is seeking to create, built around the notion that might is right and that riches and resources go to the strongest.

A high approval rate with US Catholics

Despite Trump, Leo has also been rebuilding relations with American Catholics of all stripes. No pope can write off America, as Francis sometimes seemed to do, if only because that is where much of the money to sustain the church resides. The church in the US has a formidable infrastructure of schools, universities, hospitals and charities that help shape the culture.

Loading

Leo's reconciliation is working. At the time of Trump's abusive social media post, Pew Research put the Pope's approval rating among US Catholics at 84 per cent.

A year on from his election, our first impressions remain the most lasting and revealing. Recall just moments before his appearance on the balcony of St Peter's Basilica in Rome that early evening on May 8. Cardinal Dominique Mamberti, the proto-deacon, stepped forward to reveal the name Robert Prevost and announce that he would be known as Leo XIV.

Loading...

Millions thought immediately of his namesake, Leo XIII, author of the 1891 encyclical Rerum Novarum (Of New Things). Written in the tempest of industrial change that had up-ended traditional life and rhythms, it asserted that labour should have primacy over capital and that all work should have dignity. It became the template for modern Catholic social teaching.

Leo XIV sees history at an almost identical juncture, with technology threatening to undo the economic and social gains of working people, particularly since 1945. His first encyclical, expected in days, will be on opportunities and even greater threats of artificial intelligence and technology that atomises societies and dehumanises God's children.

Leo faces a global economy more unequal, a political environment more divisive, and a world more dangerous than at any time since World War II. He will not be silent. He will not be afraid.

World.title: Entrepreneurs warn against reducing CGT discount on shares
World.content:
When Paul Bassat, the high-profile co-founder of job ad website Seek, warned on LinkedIn that the Albanese government's plan to abolish the 50 per cent discount on capital gains would be "disastrous" for entrepreneurs and "set back the startup ecosystem in Australia by a decade or more", it caused a big stir in the startup and tax community.

Some entrepreneurs see the logic in the federal government's plan to reduce the capital gains tax discount on property investments to address housing affordability, but they think the government should carve out the start-up sector.

While the CGT change has not been officially confirmed by the government, there's speculation that Treasurer Jim Chalmers will announce in Tuesday's federal budget that Labor will return to the pre-1999 inflation indexation model for capital gains for all asset classes, including property and shares.

What would you like to see in the federal budget? We want to know what issues matter to you ahead of the federal budget. Have your say.

Whether that change is grandfathered or "transitional", as some reports suggest, also remains unclear.

But what is certain is that such a change would not just stop property investors from getting a big tax break when they sell up. It would also increase the amount of tax shareholders pay if they make a gain when selling shares.

It would particularly hurt start-ups, who rely on employee share schemes to raise funds.

Paul Bassat says if there's tinkering with CGT discount for shares, "founders will leave Australia in big numbers". (ABC News)

"Founders will leave Australia in big numbers," Mr Bassat warned in a series of posts on his LinkedIn page.

"At a time when we are about to see a tsunami of job shedding by existing businesses, Australia's best hope is a wave of startup innovation. A ~50% tax on gains by founders and team members will have disastrous consequences.

" This is not about a pampered sector wanting to be treated differently but a decision about the sort of country and economy we want. "

This view was echoed by others in the tech sector who spoke to ABC News.

Why startups fear 'unintended consequences'

Startups often struggle to attract talent and conserve cash. One way to do it is to promise big returns if the startup hits Silicon Valley giant status.

For most of the time the startup runs, the company makes a loss. But the promise of a big pay day, if the company goes public or is acquired, is what enables startups to attract talent when they are competing with listed companies that can, initially, often pay far higher salaries.

Should a startup hit the status of Canva or Atlassian, that's the point that the founders and employees could choose to sell their company shares and receive a 50 per cent discount on their marginal tax rate.

Why the collapse of SVB had a 'contagion effect' The SVB collapse didn't just leave the banking sector in disarray; technology startups are bracing for a harder time, and there are fears the global economy is at risk of recession.

Doing so can be highly lucrative once companies hit multi-million-dollar valuations.

"Employee share ownership is actually a pretty powerful mechanism for retention and loyalty and hard work," says Alan Jones, a prominent Australian venture capitalist and general partner of M8 Ventures.

He told ABC News that big cash-out events for startup founders and employees "don't happen very often; they may happen once in 10 years in a startup".

Alan Jones says employee share schemes drive loyalty and hard work. (Supplied)

But asked whether that can be very lucrative for those that do cash out at the right time, he said: "Yeah, it can be. There are a number of millionaires at Canva, right?"

"But we also have to remember that the failure rate in Australian tech startups, startups worldwide, is very high."

Mr Jones thinks changes to the CGT discount would make it harder for startups to attract talent and hurt the local ecosystem.

"Why would I choose to take $200,000 in employee share options in an Australian startup and get taxed at 50 per cent. I can get paid more, pay almost no tax on my share options just for putting up with a different lifestyle in San Francisco and New York.

"Or when I can go and be a software engineer at CommBank and get very well paid, have lovely conditions … do I go and join this little five-person team that are trying to disrupt CommBank?

"Odds are most of the startups trying to disrupt CommBank will fail, but if one of them succeeds, the people who started that company have an opportunity to make good money from that. They've taken a huge risk."

Will there be a repeat of the 2009 'tax on innovation'?

Sally-Ann Williams is the former CEO at tech incubator Cicada Innovations and has worked in the sector for decades. She also fears unintended consequences.

Investors consider selling amid tax break talk With negative gearing and capital gains tax back on the national agenda, experts say such reforms would be unlikely to lead to a major fall in property prices.

"We risk repeating the disastrous 2009 Employee Share Option Plan (ESOP) 'tax on innovation', which required a six-year struggle to secure a rollback and cost Australia an entire generation of startups," Ms Williams told ABC News.

The 2009 changes to the taxation of Employee Share Schemes in Australia, referred to by some as the "tax on innovation", altered how employee shares and options were taxed, largely removing the ability to defer tax on these instruments, which severely impacted startup and growth-stage companies.

"This [possible] proposed CGT change once again penalises the very people building our future," Ms Williams said.

"At best, it is a grave unintended consequence; at worst, it is a strategic misstep that threatens to dismantle an ecosystem it has taken us decades to build.

"It's really hard to start a business and grow a business in Australia. And we don't need any additional handbrakes around that," she said.

Sally-Ann Williams says a change to the CGT discount would make it harder for startups to attract talent. (Supplied: Sally-Ann Williams)

Board director and venture capitalist investor Stephane Chatonsky also fears a change to the CGT discount could make it harder to attract talent.

"Often people move from a high-paying job to get into startups. Charging that capital at a rate of 47 per cent [assuming the employee is paying the top marginal tax rate plus the Medicare levy once they sell their shares] is tremendously unattractive," he said.

" And if the employees don't find it attractive in Australia, they'll go elsewhere. "

Carving out employee share schemes from possible CGT discount change could create 'complexity'

Mr Chatonsky says while he is supportive of changing the discount for property investors to deal with intergenerational wealth inequity, employee share schemes should be carved out.

How housing policies could shift votes As Australians head to the ballot box, the lack of affordable housing is posing a major issue for many. But the debate about how to constrain prices remains a sore point.

"Not everybody, even in Canva's situation, is going to make millions and millions of dollars. For a lot of those employees who have started discounting their salary and take risk, this is the best way and the only way to get money to pay for a deposit for a property. Not everybody is going to make tens of millions of dollars."

Ms Williams also wants the government to consider a carve out.

"There's no quick and easy fix to housing affordability, but let's not make sure that unintended consequences of trying to fix that then also put the handbrakes on business growth," she said.

But The Tax Institute's tax counsel John Storey says while there are merits to look at changes to the CGT discount, simplicity has to be a factor and any changes should apply to all asset classes.

He says carving out startups using employee share schemes would be complicated because it would mean "different rules apply for different assets".

"There shouldn't be carve outs. It will make a complex tax system far more complex," Mr Storey said.

"Are we just talking small business? Do we use existing definitions of small business? It does create all sorts of complexities."

Mr Storey says there are other concessions for small businesses that can help reduce the capital gains, but "it's not the next inventor of Google who cashes out for a billion dollars".

COVID-time loss carry-back scheme may be back on the table

To help maintain business investment, Tuesday's budget could also include a loss carry-back scheme that allows incorporated businesses to "carry back" losses from the current financial year against previously taxed profits.

During the pandemic, businesses that had aggregated turnover of up to $5 billion were able to carry back losses for several years and get big refunds, and there are suggestions the government may be looking at it again.

Some entrepreneurs think the government should carve out the startup sector if the CGT discount changes. (Unsplash: Annie Spratt)

FinTech Australia CEO Rehan D'Almeida welcomes any moves to reinstate the loss carry-back scheme, modelled on the measure that ran during the pandemic.

"Carry-back is one of the most cash-flow effective levers available to early-stage and scaling fintechs, which routinely cycle between profit and loss years as they invest in growth, talent and product," he said.

But he also remained concerned about the proposed changes to CGT discount for startups.

"Penalising this type of incentive will damage the technology sector," he said.

"The fintech sector already supports over 50,000 jobs directly and 100,000 jobs indirectly, and these changes could pose a threat to these roles."

Mr D'Almeida said the group was also opposed to a proposal to lift the minimum threshold for the Research and Development Tax Incentive claim.

"The current threshold is an important means of incentivising local R&D by startups and further risks driving them offshore," he said.

World.title: What the tax reform duo could mean for renters
World.content:
The federal government is expected to use next week's budget to wind back negative gearing and the capital gains tax (CGT) discount, two taxation instruments favoured by property investors.

It is an idea that featured in Labor's failed 2019 campaign.

However, there has long been speculation about its revival.

Now, the ABC has confirmed the taxes would form the centrepiece of a budget targeted at young voters.

But Australia's biggest industry groups, economists and housing policy experts caution that any changes made may inadvertently push rents higher.

So we spoke to three experts who explained, in theory, what any housing tax policy changes could mean for renters.

First, catch me up

Over the past few months, the federal government has laid down the groundwork for changes to the CGT discount and negative gearing concessions in its federal budget next week.

When asked last Tuesday about the changes, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the issue of intergenerational equity was important.

"In Australian society, what we know is that for many young people, they feel like they haven't got a fair crack compared with my generation and the generations beforehand," Mr Albanese said.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese appreciates the issue of intergenerational equity. ( )

The ABC has since reported that there would likely be full grandfathering for negative gearing, but partial for the CGT discount.

Here is a breakdown of how they work and the expected changes.

What changes will be made to negative gearing? Read more What is it? Negative gearing is when investment property owners operate at a loss, typically because the mortgage payments and other costs are higher than the rental income. They then deduct that loss from their overall taxable income to reduce their income tax payable. The changes Negative gearing changes are expected to be fully grandfathered, according to several sources. But it is unclear whether the policy will cap the number of negatively geared properties, limit negative gearing to newly built properties, or phase it out entirely in future. What changes will be made to the CGT discount? Read more What is it? Capital gains tax is paid when an investment property (or share) is sold, with the gain currently taxed at 50 per cent of a person's ordinary tax rate. The "gain" is the amount an asset has increased in value since it was purchased, with some adjustments. The changes The CGT discount is likely to be reverted to the pre-1999 scheme, which made the discount equal to the amount of inflation over the life of the asset, but Labor may also consider a flat discount such as 25, 30 or 35 per cent. An important design question is whether the policy will be fully grandfathered, so that the old rules are retained indefinitely for all existing assets, or whether there will be some transition to the new rules. What is grandfathering? Read more Grandfathering (or a grandfather clause) is a provision where an old rule continues to apply to existing situations while a new rule applies to all future cases.

Some experts say the tax changes could stall the supply of new rental homes at a time of surging population growth due to migration.

Could it affect rental prices?

It likely will.

Recent modelling commissioned by property lobby groups showed new home building would slow and rents would rise under a range of scenarios.

Modelling for the property industry by economic firms Qaive and Tulipwood Economics found that combining a CGT discount cut with negative gearing restrictions could slash dwelling starts — housing construction — by tens of thousands of homes, pushing rents 2.4 per cent higher by 2029-30.

But the view among economists is that price rises won't be "supercharged".

PRD chief economist Diaswati Mardiasmo told the ABC rental prices won't rocket to the likes of what we saw post-COVID.

"We saw rents supercharge post-COVID by 20-25 per cent because there were no investors playing in the market and there were a lot of people trying to find a rental property," Dr Mardiasmo said.

"I don't believe we will see prices increase to that extent."

Diaswati Mardiasmo says rental prices should not skyrocket. ( )

Robert Carling, a senior fellow in economics at the Centre for Independent Studies, shared a similar view.

"Winding back negative gearing will make investment in rental housing less attractive, the supply of such housing will decline, and rents will increase," Professor Carling told the ABC.

"However, I would not expect large effects from the kinds of changes that are rumoured."

‍Cotality's Rental Review Q1 2026 shows national dwelling rents increased 2.1 per cent over the three months to March, up from a 1.2 per cent increase in Q4 2025.

The median weekly rent for homes across Australia's capital cities is $724 per week. Across the regions, the median rent is $612.

Curtin University economics professor Rachel ViforJ says for every investment property that is sold by landlords, that is one extra property available in the market for purchase by aspiring homebuyers.

"Even if rents rise in the short run, over time it should fall or stabilise as more people are able to buy their own homes," Professor ViforJ told the ABC.

'Devil in the details'

Dr Mardiasmo says whether we see any significant effect on rental prices, and when, will come down to "the devil in the details".

Professor Carling agrees.

In this case, they are referring to grandfathering (remember the term we defined above?).

Grandfathering means any new changes to negative gearing or how CGT is taxed won't apply to any investment properties that are bought prior to a particular date.

Negative gearing, CGT and trusts explained The government is poised to make changes to negative gearing, the capital gains tax discount and the tax treatment of trusts. So how do they work, and what could changes look like?

For example, if the federal government says it is grandfathering negative gearing and it applies to properties bought before the budget, then that means it only applies to investment properties that people buy from that date onwards.

So it is not going to apply to properties that are already on the market and properties that investors already own.

In theory, one way the CGT discount could be partially grandfathered would be to tax gains made before a date set by the government at 50 per cent, while gains after would be taxed differently.

This is why Dr Mardiasmo and Professor Carling believe any flow-on effects to rental prices won't be sudden — they will lag anywhere between six and 12 months.

"If existing investments are protected from the changes, the impact on rents will be less and it will be more drawn out over time," Professor Carling said.

Even under all scenarios, existing renters likely currently have their rents locked in for six months to a year due to existing lease agreements.

Approximately 2.2 million Australians owned at least one investment property in 2020-21, according to the ATO.

Around 70 per cent of those hold one investment property, while 18 per cent hold two and 5 per cent hold three.

Don't forget about rising interest rates

On Tuesday, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) announced the cash rate will increase by 0.25 percentage points to 4.35 per cent.

It is the third time in a row the RBA has lifted its cash rate target, and there is every possible chance another could be coming our way later this year.

Successive rate rises could have a larger impact on rental prices than tax reforms for two reasons, Professor ViforJ said.

"First, many landlords owe a mortgage debt on their rental properties, so if rates continue to rise, they will raise rents to meet higher mortgage repayments," she said.

"Second, as rates rise, homebuyers will find their borrower capacity decline, so many might wait for interest rates to fall before looking to make a home purchase.

"If this happens, there will be more competition in the rental sector as people remain longer in the rental market."

World.title: Australia on cusp of housing downturn as demand softens
World.content:
The tight supply conditions that have underpinned the national housing market in recent years are starting to ease, according to property data firm Cotality.

This, combined with a softening in demand, has created the conditions for a national property market downturn.

Cotality research director Tim Lawless said Sydney and Melbourne were already five months into the early phases of decline, while growth was slowing across the mid-sized capitals.

"Listings are picking up as demand softens, interest rates are rising, while affordability and serviceability pressures are biting," he said.

Cotality research shows that, historically, there have been several catalysts for housing declines, including global shocks, rising interest rates, and periods of credit tightening, as well as changes in fiscal policy and broader market factors such as affordability and sentiment.

Independent economist Saul Eslake agrees that some elements are in place for continued weakness in the housing market.

Saul Eslake agrees a housing downturn is possible. (ABC: Maren Preuss)

"It is quite plausible that the combination of higher interest rates and greater caution on the part of prospective buyers [prompted by apprehension about the economic consequences of the conflict in the Middle East] could see a downturn in property prices."

This, he said, comes despite "the ongoing mismatch between the 'underlying' demand for housing and the supply of it."

In other words, demand is softening sufficiently to overwhelm the existing lack of supply and the upward pressure that naturally puts on prices.

"[A lack of supply] has been a characteristic of Australian housing markets for most of the past 30 years — but it hasn't prevented occasional downturns in the effective [as distinct from the underlying] demand for housing from causing brief periods of price declines," Mr Eslake said.

Put another way, "it's the effective demand for housing — what people are willing and able to pay — interacting with the supply of housing, not the 'underlying' demand [determined by population growth and household formation rates] — that matters for movements in prices over short periods."

Melbourne property values declined in April. (Supplied: Victorian government)

Capital city prices to decline

With capital city home values only 0.2 per cent higher in April, and fading, Tim Lawless, Cotality's Asia Pacific head of research, said there was a good chance the combined capitals index would move into decline over the coming months as further momentum leaves the market.

"This trend has been amplified by 75 basis points [0.75 percentage points] of rate hikes so far this year and the chance of another hike, or hikes, later in the year," he said.

What would you like to see in the federal budget? We want to know what issues matter to you ahead of the federal budget. Have your say.

"Importantly, the market was already slowing well before the hiking cycle commenced, highlighting the downside impact of waning confidence from late last year alongside rising inflation and worsening levels of housing affordability."

Sydney dwelling values fell 0.6 per cent in April and are now 1.0 per cent below their November 2025 peak.

Melbourne values declined 0.6 per cent over the month and sit 2.3 per cent below their March 2022 high.

More vendors are now coming to market.

New listings have increased, with 39,319 properties added over the four weeks to early May, which is 4.7 per cent above the five-year average.

Total listings remain below average levels, at 127,821 properties nationally, down 2.6 per cent from a year ago.

Cotality noted that listing levels are increasing as buyer demand softens rather than because of a surge in new stock coming onto the market.

The total stock of advertised properties remains low nationally, but is rising, and holding at above average levels in Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra.

Recent buyers at risk of 'negative equity'

Cotality's report also noted that "more recent buyers are likely to be exposed to the risk of negative equity as values fall, particularly those who entered the market with smaller deposits, including participants who took advantage of the Australian Government 5% Deposit Scheme."

Negative equity occurs when the outstanding balance of a loan (such as a mortgage or car loan) is higher than the current market value of the asset securing it.

"Recent buyers are arguably at more risk of seeing negative equity, given they have had less time to accrue value in their property or pay down the principal of their loan," Mr Lawless said.

Those who have purchased homes recently could become victims of negative equity, Cotality warns. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"However, mortgage repayments are typically prioritised, with borrowers more likely to adjust spending elsewhere before missing a payment."

And Mr Eslake said history shows policymakers are attuned to the plight of those facing negative equity.

“Those periods of price declines have all been fairly brief because whenever they have occurred, governments have responded to fears that 'the sky will fall in' [if house prices are allowed to fall substantially] by doing things designed to stop house prices from falling, such as doubling or trebling first home owners' grants, and encouraging the RBA to cut interest rates,” he said.

"Yes, it's probable that some people would find themselves in a 'negative equity' position … but as long as those folks keep their jobs, and hence can afford to continue to service their mortgages, they'll be OK in the long run."

Ongoing strength in some markets

Pockets of strength remain within the national housing market.

Perth values rose 26.0 per cent over the past year compared to just 2.0 per cent in Melbourne, with the gap in annual growth rates across the capital cities widening to 24 percentage points.

"An expectation that labour markets will remain tight, as well as a history of stringent prudential standards, including the three-percentage point mortgage serviceability buffer, should help to keep mortgage arrears low as interest rates rise," Mr Lawless said.

Mortgage repayments calculator Our mortgage repayment calculator will show you how much your loan repayments may change.

Indeed, the combined capitals Home Value Index has risen 33.7 per cent over the past five years, with markets such as Perth, Brisbane and Adelaide recording growth of around 80 per cent to 90 per cent over the same period.

"Historically, housing downturns have been relatively short-lived, with all but three capital city downturns over the past 40 years lasting less than 12 months, although the length and magnitude have varied from city to city," he said.

And, according to auctioneer Dennis Nutt, investors continue looking for value in the market.

"There's always investors in the market waiting — waiting for deals," he said.

"We're in that type of market now.

"We have vendors who may have purchased four years ago at the height of the market, [who] now, for whatever circumstances, need to sell."

Reality check for aspiring first home buyers

While the property market is turning, academics say it does not necessarily open the door to improved housing affordability.

A professor of urban and regional planning at Sydney University, Nicole Gurran, told the ABC, "People who most need to get into home ownership are least able to get a loan when prices fall dramatically.

"It's really an economic shock that triggers a dramatic downturn in property prices."

In this environment, Professor Gurran argued, "People can't afford to borrow [to buy a home] because they don't have stable incomes."

And, she added, lower-income households still have competition at the bottom end of the rental market.

World.title: ISIS-linked women willing to take the 'hit' of arrests for their kids' freedom
World.content:
When a group of Australian women and children linked to ISIS boarded a flight from Doha to Melbourne on Wednesday, they took a leap of faith, unsure of what fate awaited them at the end of their journey.

Those 14 hours in the air would either mark the beginning of their new lives, or the end of their brief freedom.

"We just want the children to be safe," one of the women explained to the ABC as she waited at the airport.

In the arrivals' terminal in Doha, the women weren't hard to miss, despite their oversized sunglasses and hijabs, as their thick Australian accents carried across the room.

Kawsar Abbas, her daughters Zeinab Ahmed and Zahra Ahmed, and their children were accompanied by their uncle, Melbourne Boxing Coach Abraham Abbas, who had travelled to Syria to help bring them home.

After initially showing hostility to media waiting at the gate, the women quickly warmed.

Part of the group boarded a connecting flight from Doha to Melbourne. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

They joked they should have spoken in Arabic to blend in, after the ABC approached them as they transited the city on their way to Melbourne. They had just arrived from Damascus.

They were almost giddy, telling the ABC this would be the first time their children — one dressed in a Spiderman T-shirt — who were born in Syria would visit Australia.

The group have been trapped in legal and political limbo for more than seven years after they were captured by US-backed Kurdish forces during the fall of Islamic State and placed in dusty detention camps in Syria's desert.

Inside one facility the small group had formed a small enclave with other Australians, called Australia Street. They were drawn together by their shared nationality and a longing to return home, as well as a feeling that the camp was no place for a child.

The Al Roj refugee camp (pictured in February) houses people who were displaced by the fall of Islamic State. (ABC News: Baderkhan Ahmad)

Their children, many of whom had never been outside of Syria, dreamed of distant shores, and of the small treasures that might await them there.

"It's like paradise for them," another of the woman told the ABC.

"They've already asked if they can have a PlayStation 5."

From February: Children in Syrian camp dream of tasting ice cream in Australia The children of women with ISIS links stuck in a Syrian refugee camp talk about their attempt to leave the camp in February, saying they dream of one day buying toys and ice cream in Australia.

The younger cohort from Syria became visibly excited when they got to Gate C9 at Qatar's airport. Feelings remained high when they joined the queue lining up to board and for most of the flight home.

But hanging over the women in the group were serious allegations about their time in Syria, as a day earlier the Australian Federal Police (AFP) had warned some of them could face slavery- or terrorism-related charges upon arrival.

On the flight, the women used the onboard WiFi to constantly scroll the news for live updates on their situation.

They learnt that two of them would likely face arrest in Australia.

As the plane approached Tullamarine airport on Thursday, the mood quickly shifted from one of hope to slight concern.

But they all remained calm, telling the ABC they were prepared for whatever would greet them at the airport.

Loading...

Life in a camp

In the early 2010s Islamic State drew tens of thousands of supporters from around the world to fight or to live in what was billed as a pure Islamic society.

Many were women who were brought by their husbands or fathers, some came alone and married, others were forced to marry after they arrived. Many of these women had their own fundamentalist views and travelled there willingly.

The group's so-called caliphate was defeated in 2019 by a US-led coalition, and many of the men who had travelled to serve were killed or captured. Their wives and children were taken to camps, and many of them have remained there ever since.

In the Al Roj camp, thousands of people, most originally from abroad, live in squalid conditions. Dozens of Australians have left in recent years, but it is understood that 21 still remain in the camp.

All 34 women and children tried to leave the Al Roj camp in February, but were quickly forced to turn back. (ABC News: Baderkhan Ahmad)

The outlook inside the camp has been bleak for many years, but recently a window of opportunity opened when Kurdish-led forces began reluctantly handing over control to Syrian government forces following their successful military offensive.

Syria seized another camp, Al Hol, in January, prompting many detainees to flee as the Kurds retreated. Al Roj still remains controlled by the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), but after repeatedly asking foreign countries to repatriate their citizens, its officials have been letting detainees with travel documents leave.

Kawsar, Zeinab and Zahra — as well as another woman, Janai Safar, who flew to Sydney separately with her child — left the Al Roj camp on April 24.

They were part of a broader group of 34 women and children living in the camp, who briefly made it out in January after securing Australian passports. At that time, they didn't make it far before they were forced to turn back by Syrian authorities.

Not long after, advocates, lawyers and family members travelled to Damascus for crisis talks with Syrian officials, where they argued the cohort were Australian citizens, had travel documents, and could not be legally blocked from returning to Australia.

Not wanted

The Kurdish administration in northern Syria and international humanitarian organisations have long urged countries such as Australia to repatriate their citizens and their children, both for their own welfare and to help resolve the problem inside Syrian camps.

Experts had argued that if the women were accused of any crimes in Syria, they should be dealt with in their home countries.

According to Save the Children, about 180 people were repatriated by eight countries, including Spain, France, and Canada, last year. Several other nations are still working out what to do about their citizens, many of whom have been in the camp for years.

But in Australia, there's little sympathy for their plight, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese making his contempt for the IS-linked Australians abundantly clear, declaring the women had "made their bed" and must now "lie in it".

Loading...

"They made an appalling, disgraceful decision," Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said on Wednesday, of the original move by the women to travel to Syria.

"These are horrific situations that have been brought on those children by the actions of their parents."

The uncle who travelled with the women believes they have been unfairly demonised by the Australian government and the Australian public.

"The Australian government doesn't want to know about them," he said.

How a window opened for IS-linked Australians to leave Syria After holding a large swathe of autonomous territory that included two detention camps, Kurdish-led forces are now reluctantly handing over control to Syrian government forces, following their successful military offensive.

Criminologists have previously told the ABC the welfare of the children should be prioritised and the families returned for that reason.

"The longer [younger children spend] in that sort of environment, the more chance they will be influenced by that environment," ANU criminologist Clarke Jones, who has worked extensively in the field of extremism, told the ABC last February.

"The sooner the Australian government gets them out of those camps and brings them back to face the criminal justice system or other sorts of support, the better off they'll be."

The group walking through Melbourne Airport, before reaching the chaos on the other side of immigration. (ABC News)

The women told the ABC they were willing to take the "hit" of arrest for the sake of their children, after living in what they described as "hell" in the Al Roj camp.

So far, only one woman has been issued with a Temporary Exclusion Order, banning her from travelling to Australia for two years on national security grounds.

The ABC understands that woman is still in the Al Roj refugee camp in Syria, along with other Australian women and children who are waiting to come home.

An uncertain future

After landing in Australia on Thursday night, the women and children stepped off the plane to begin their new lives.

They were the last ones off the flight, refusing to disembark until the media on board had, requesting not to be photographed.

They walked through customs until they got to immigration where they spent more than two hours.

As the group exited at the arrivals hall, they had a group of a dozen men in black suits waiting to help escort them.

A huge media scrum armed with cameras and microphones pounced on the group as they battled their way through the terminal to a waiting white mini-van.

A large media scrum were at Melbourne airport to greet the group. (ABC News: Kate Ashton)

The children were carried out, visibly upset at the chaos.

After landing in Melbourne and Sydney and getting through immigration, police quickly swooped in.

Kawsar Abbas, 53, and Zeinab Ahmed, 31, were arrested on slave-related charges, while Janai Safar, 32, was arrested on charges related to being affiliated with terrorism.

Janai Safar was arrested by police upon her arrival in Sydney. (ABC News)

Zahra Ahmed, 33, has not been charged.

While their future remains uncertain, the women said they felt a surge of relief when the plane touched down on Australian soil, after years of trying to escape Syria.

They told the ABC their next task is to get the remainder of the 21 women and children who are in the Al Roj refugee back home too, and they'll start that in coming weeks.

World.title: Sir David Attenborough turns 100: Celebrate his life in his words
World.content:
British broadcaster Sir David Attenborough has brought the natural world to living rooms for the past seven decades.

But what does he have to say about this extraordinary life of adventure?

To celebrate his 100th birthday, we look back at his work and interviews to capture in his words some of the wisdom and endless sense of wonder that has made him a household name.

The young fossil hunter

A natural sense of wonderment drove Sir David's early childhood explorations around the English countryside during the interwar period.

As he told the BBC documentary Attenborough's Journey in 2010:

"When I was a boy growing up in the Midlands in Leicester, the rocks and limestones you found in the east of the country were full of the most magical things.

"You hit a stone and it suddenly fell open and there was this amazing coiled shell. Beautiful and extraordinary and nobody had seen that for 150 million years except you.

"So I thought it was very romantic and exciting and it appealed to the small boy's instinct of collecting things, to be honest I don't think I've really lost [it]."

Sir David has been an avid collector of ammonites and fossils since he was a boy. (Flickr: Kara Stenberg, Ammonite, CC BY-NC 2.0)

Fossils were just one of the curiosities a young Sir David kept, as he recalled on BBC Radio 4 in 2009:

"I had a small museum as a boy, many boys do.

"Mine contained a Victorian bun penny, a shed skin of a grass snake, some fossil ammonites, a twisted piece of metal from an incendiary bomb that had been dropped on Leicester where I lived — for this was during the war — and a small brown object two-and-a-quarter inches long. I can be quite precise about its measurements because I still have it.

" It is ... a piece of amber, and I was given it by a girl, a refugee from Nazi oppression who, in 1938, stayed in our house for a few weeks on her way to relatives in the United States. "

He also has fond memories of his first pet: a fire salamander that was given to him on his eighth birthday by his father.

A fire salamander was Sir David's first pet and he would make a family tradition by giving them to his own children. (iNaturalist: Borna Tonković, Fire salamander, CC BY-NC 4.0)

" The most remarkable thing about it to my young eyes was its colour. It was a dramatic glossy black with brilliant sulphur-yellow blotches. It seemed as glamorous and as spectacular to me as any tropical species. "

Early career

Sir David completed a natural sciences degree at the University of Cambridge before being called up for two years of national service in 1947.

Afterwards, he married his wife Jane, who he met at university, and got a position in educational publishing.

Adventures to far-flung destinations occupied Sir David's mind, so he decided to apply for a radio job at the BBC.

Sir David had only watched a television once before he got a traineeship with the BBC. (Getty Images: Popperfoto)

But, as he wrote in his memoirs, Life on Air, he didn't get the job. Then, someone else from the BBC called and asked if he was interested in a television role:

" I had to confess that I hadn't actually seen much television. I had once watched a television play in my wife's parents' house, but they were the only people I knew with a set and I certainly had not got one myself. "

Sir David took a chance, quit his job and underwent a three-month BBC traineeship with no guarantee of employment at the end.

"I had managed to make myself sufficiently useful to be offered a further six-month employment, this time as a full-blown assistant producer. So my time as a member of the BBC's staff began."

Bringing nature to TV screens

Sir David produced black-and-white shows that were filmed in a studio. Then, in the 1950s, he came up with an idea to film rare animals abroad in their own environment with the London Zoo's reptiles curator Jack Lester.

He figured the Zoo would benefit from the publicity of sending a TV crew on an expedition and convinced the BBC they would benefit from the experience.

The show was called Zoo Quest and would take Sir David to Sierra Leone where a range of animals were filmed and then captured to be housed in London Zoo:

" As well as snakes, there were bush babies and bird-eating spiders, tortoises and chameleons, sunbirds, owl chicks and parrots. Jack was particularly pleased with a dozen or so emerald starlings, spectacularly beautiful glossy green birds, that are only found in a small area of West Africa, for they would be a species new to the zoo's collections. "

Sir David shows a then Prince Charles and Princess Anne a cockatoo on Zoo Quest in 1958. (Getty Images: Central Press)

Jack Lester was supposed to be the star of the show but he fell ill during the filming of the first two seasons of Zoo Quest.

Sir David stepped up to host segments of the program where animals caught during the trips were shown up close in a studio.

Sadly Lester died young at 47 after the second season, but Zoo Quest trips continued. Sir David ventured to countries like Guyana, New Guinea, Paraguay and Tonga to film animals like orangutans, armadillos and Komodo dragons.

Sir David in Australia

He first visited Australia in the 1960s, where he filmed art, culture and interviews with First Nations people.

"We would also be able to find a rich range of animals — marsupials like wallabies and bandicoots, gorgeous birds and bizarre reptiles," Sir David wrote in Life on Air.

"Today a national park complete with luxury hotels has been established there and given the name of Kakadu, after the Aboriginal people whose homeland it is. At that time, however, the whole areas was referred to vaguely, if at all, as the Top End."

Australia has a special place in Sir David's heart as he reflected on in 2015 with the release of a Great Barrier Reef documentary:

North Queensland is Sir David's favourite place on Earth — besides home — with its rainforests, mountains and the Great Barrier Reef. (Supplied)

"I'm asked actually frequently, 'Where is your favourite place in the world?'. I start off by saying home, [they say] 'But if not home where would it be?', and I usually say, not just this occasion but many occasions, 'actually North Queensland'.

"North Queensland is a wonderful, wonderful place, it's got everything. It's got mountains, it's got tropical rainforest, it's got the [Great] Barrier Reef, it's got wonderful creatures that occur nowhere else. It's a great place."

Boss of BBC 2

Sir David went freelance in 1962 after his first Australian work trip.

He wanted to spend half his time filming and the other half studying anthropology.

In 1965, as he recalled in Life on Air, the BBC came calling with an offer to run the newish TV channel BBC 2:

" I said I would take the job provided I was able to make a program of some kind every 18 months or so — just to keep in touch with the latest technologies and techniques. "

Sir David in 1965 after being appointed the new head of BBC2. (Getty Images: David Cairns/Daily Express/Hulton Archive)

Sir David set the tone for what BBC2 should be in offering programs unlike anything else on television.

Not only did he decide the network should be the first in the world to fund an archaeological dig, he also ushered in colour television for British screens:

"The BBC had produced the first public television service in the world in 1936. The United States and Japan had preceded us into colour but at least the BBC could be the first in Europe to transmit in colour. But how? Wimbledon provided the answer. With both our colour outside broadcast units installed at the tennis championships, we could produce several hours of colour transmissions every day. And we would be ahead of our rivals."

Sir David oversaw the introduction of hit colour shows like Civilisation, which looked at major European artworks, and Pot Black, a popular snooker program.

Life on Earth

Sir David went freelance again in the 1970s.

After completing a seven-part series on tribal art he was approached by the BBC to helm a major nature program.

His plan was a 13-episode series:

" I would start at the beginning of life, trace the long story of its evolution as both plants and animals spread from the sea and on to the land in increasingly complex forms. "

"We would use living species to illustrate how fish hauled themselves out of the water and became amphibians, like newts, frogs and toads. Early amphibians, in turn, developed impermeable skins and so gave rise to the reptiles. Ancient reptiles, such as dinosaurs, developed warm blood and eventually gave rise to mammals.

"The series would end with monkeys, apes and mankind."

Sir David interacts with an orangutan and her baby at London Zoo in 1982. (Getty Images: mirror/Mirror pix)

This ambitious program was Life on Earth in 1979 which established him as a household name around the globe.

The penultimate episode titled "Life in the Trees" captured one of the most significant moments of his career at Dian Fossey's Rwandan gorilla sanctuary.

Crawling towards the sounds of feeding mountain gorillas he came eye to eye with an adult female and delivered one of television history's most impactful moments:

"There is more meaning and mutual understanding in exchanging a glance with a gorilla than any other animal I know.

"We're so similar. Their sight, their hearing, their sense of smell, is so similar to ours that we see the world in the same way they do. They live in the same sort of social groups, and form permanent family relationships. They walk along on the ground as we do though they are immensely more powerful than we are.

"It seems really very unfair that man should have chosen the gorilla to symbolise everything that is aggressive and violent, when that is the one thing that the gorilla is not — and that we are."

Becoming TV's face of nature

Sir David hopes we can all live harmoniously with nature. (Getty Images: John Stillwell/PA Images)

Life on Earth would become a 20-year project with more documentaries falling under the banner of the "Life" series.

The 79-episode journey ended in 2008 with Life in Cold Blood, which looked at amphibians and reptiles in depth.

Sir David, 81 at the time, spoke in a BBC radio interview when the series ended about what he hoped its legacy would be:

"If you'd asked me 20 years ago whether we'd be attempting such a mammoth task, I'd have said 'Don't be ridiculous'. These programs tell a particular story and I'm sure others will come along and tell it much better than I did."

" But I do hope that if people watch it in 50 years' time, it will still have something to say about the world we live in. "

Even after the decades it took to tell Earth's evolutionary history through the 79 episodes of the Life series, Sir David is still making natural history documentaries. (Supplied)

There has been no such thing, however, as retirement for Sir David.

While he may not write and spearhead programs as much as he used to, he has continued to present and narrate documentaries.

And, as with Galapagos 3D in 2013, he has continued to capture the immensity of nature and its fragility.

Here he talks about Lonesome George, the last Pinta tortoise in the world, which died 14 days after Sir David filmed with him in 2012.

Lonesome George was the last of his kind, a Pinta Galapagos tortoise that died in 2012. (Reuters: Guillermo Granja)

" He's about 80 years old and he's getting a bit creaky in his joints, as indeed am I.When he dies, the Pinta species of Galapagos tortoise will be extinct. But he is a very important animal, probably more than any other single creature he's focused the attention of the world on the fragility of our environment and he's stimulated science to look into whole new areas of research here in the Galapagos. "

Reaching icon status

Along with being knighted twice, Sir David's contribution as a naturalist and documentary maker has been recognised by scientists around the world.

Over the years, more than 50 species and genera of plants, animals, microorganisms and ancient life-forms named after him. The most recent is a species of wasp, which was named after him for his 100th birthday.

But he does have a favourite, he revealed in an interview with the Washington Post in 2015:

" There are quite a lot of species. To have a species named after you, and attenboroughi species, that's quite nice. But to have a genus named after you is really something else. And there's a family of aquatic reptiles which was given my name which is Attenborosaurus. Attenborosaurus is really something isn't it. "

What was thought to be a plesiosaur fossil in 1880 was reclassified in 1993 as Attenborosaurus conybeari. (Biodiversity Heritage Library: Philibert Charles Berjeau)

A voice for the environment

On reflecting on his career in the first edition of his memoir in 2003, Sir David wrote about why he made his documentaries:

" I did not make them because I had premonitions of impending eco-disaster. I did so because I know of no pleasure deeper than that which comes from contemplating the natural world and trying to understand it. "

Sir David has travelled the globe to document creatures great and small, like the mighty but miniture-sized Atlas beetle. (Supplied)

But that doesn't mean he has shied away from talking about humankind's responsibilities. At an Australian Museum lecture hosted by The Science Show's Robyn Williams in 1991 he said:

"We are the most remarkable species the world has ever seen, certainly the most complex and undoubtedly the most powerful. And that, it seems to me, puts a great responsibility in our hands because we can determine the life and death of a species.

"If films like these perhaps underline that responsibility and that ... relationship with the rest of the natural world, then I think all of us cameramen, scientists, directors, producers and presenters would be very happy."

An advocate for science

Sir David and The Science Show host Robyn Williams. (ABC Science: David Fisher)

Sir David has been a regular guest on The Science Show with Williams, including a 2012 episode where he talked about the politicisation of science:

"I think it's very disturbing indeed that when you get a message from science that you don't like, you say, 'Well, the science is wrong.'

"That's not what science is about.

"Science is about looking unblinkingly at the facts, and when they don't match what you thought, then you change the way you think."

A lifelong voyage to understanding

Now near the end of his life, Sir David still hopes to inspire humanity to live in harmony with nature. (Supplied: Disney+)

And as he reached 100 years on the planet, Sir David still encouraged people through his documentaries, like last year's film Ocean, to live sustainably with nature:

"Through the course of my life, we have been on a voyage of ocean discovery. And what a journey it has been.

"When I first saw the sea as a young boy, it was thought of as a vast wilderness to be tamed and mastered for the benefit of humanity. Now, as I approach the end of my life, we know the opposite is true.

"It is my great hope that we all come to see the ocean not as a dark and distant place with little relevance to our lives on land, but as the lifeblood of our home. I'm sure that nothing is more important. For if we save the sea, we save our world."

You can celebrate Sir David Attenborough’s 100th birthday by watching a selection of thought-provoking and landmark documentaries on ABC iview.

World.title: Why did my workplace agree to an idea we knew would fail?
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceWork therapy Opinion Why did my workplace agree to an idea we knew would fail? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor May 8, 2026 — 5:10am

May 8, 2026 — 5:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

During a meeting, our team had to decide on the best way to handle a complex project. We worked constructively through several parts. After one vital question, there was a long moment of silence followed by laughter. It was obvious we had come upon the most difficult part of the plan. After a long pause, a member of our team proposed a solution – I’ll call it Idea X. Again there was silence. Again there was laughter. We finally decided it was a good idea and moved on. The project is now under way and Idea X has turned out to be disastrous. The amazing thing is that everyone in that meeting, including the person who proposed it, admits now they knew it was a terrible idea. How could we have let this happen? Why did nobody say anything? If it seems like a bad idea at the time, it might be worth speaking up. John Shakespeare I think you might have encountered the Abilene paradox. It’s an idea that was advanced by a social psychologist and professor of management scientist from the United States called Jerry B. Harvey. The name comes from an anecdote about his family. Harvey and his wife were on holiday at her parents’ home in Texas and were having a lazy afternoon – playing dominoes and drinking cooled lemonade – on an extremely hot day. Harvey’s father-in-law suggested they go to Abilene, a town almost 100 kilometres away, for dinner.



Everyone agreed. They drove through the desert in a car without air-conditioning as the temperature reached 40 degrees. The food, when they got there, was unpleasant. When they returned to the holiday house after hours in the oppressively hot vehicle, everyone admitted they hadn’t wanted to go in the first place. Editor's pick Opinion

Careers For this career move, getting older is actually an advantage Tim Duggan Work columnist What Harvey realised when he reflected on the strange occurrence was that the problem came about because of a series of assumptions, poor communication and a desire to avoid being “ostracised”. While the anecdote reads like something from a Raymond Carver short story in which repressed, over-polite 1970s Americans suffer in silence, there’s strong evidence to suggest the problem is more generalisable, and is pertinent to modern workplaces. In the 1970s family account, the father-in-law suggests they go on this ill-advised trip because he worries the family is bored and sees himself as responsible for the holiday. In your case, I suspect the person who proposed the idea made a different kind of assumption: that the long pause and awkward laughter required a decisive response. I also suspect they are a senior member of the team and so felt obligated to deliver that response.



In both the Abilene story and your situation, the assumptions were wrong. The family were not bored – they were inactive because of the heat but content. Similarly, your team did not desperately require an answer there and then. They needed to accept that they had hit, as you said, the most challenging aspect of the project, a knot that couldn’t be undone in a single meeting. Harvey would call what happened an “inability to manage agreement” (as opposed to conflict). Even though every single person in the room knew (or at least retrospectively professed to know) that the answer was deeply flawed, they agreed to it. Why did nobody say anything? Almost certainly due to internal assumptions. And this is where the fear of ostracism comes in. How did you let this happen? The paradox helps to explain it but not necessarily how to avoid it next time. To achieve that, I think you need to understand what motivated each person in the room to agree. Was it over-politeness? Did people desperately want to avoid seeming ungracious? Did they feel that denigrating the person willing to offer something at an uncomfortable juncture in the meeting was worse than jeopardising the project? Or are there slightly more sinister reasons? Did people keep their mouths shut because they had good reason to believe they would be punished, looked down upon or labelled “difficult”? Was the awkward silence and laughter a product of a workplace devoid of psychological safety?



Meanwhile, have a read of Harvey’s article. It’s more than 50 years old, but I think it remains as relevant as ever. Send your questions through to Work Therapy by emailing jonathan@theinkbureau.com.au

World.title: Sydney has an image problem. Here is how we fix it
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life Sydney has an image problem. Here is how we fix it Megan Gorrey May 8, 2026 — 5:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney is missing out on $3.3 billion a year because it is often perceived on the world stage as little more than a picturesque holiday destination defined by its architectural landmarks and beaches. The view that Sydney’s appeal did not extend beyond the Opera House, Harbour Bridge and Bondi Beach was outdated and vastly undersold the depth and diversity of the NSW capital, risking a drain of investors, talent, and visitors, a new report from the Committee for Sydney think tank has found. Sydney’s iconic landmarks are instantly recognisable, but they don’t tell the whole story, the report argues. Wolter Peeters Committee chief executive Eamon Waterford said Sydney was “really well-regarded on the world stage” for its landmarks and natural landscapes. “The problem is, it’s only a tiny bit of Sydney,” he said. “The Sydney we sell to the world is experienced by a very small number of Sydneysiders, and the city we all know and love is not at all part of the story we tell the world.”



The committee’s Beyond the Postcard report, published on Friday, said Sydney lacked a consistent, citywide strategy beyond the visitor economy and needed to tell a more complete and compelling narrative – or it would lose relevance, investment and global influence to better-positioned cities. Related Article City life Nightlife v the arts: Report finds NSW cultural priorities are ‘out of balance’ The report is the next step in the committee’s Sydney Global project, launched in 2025, which aimed to create a clear, shared narrative for Sydney to address concerns that the city was not well understood. It said a strong brand was a form of soft power that could give cities a competitive edge globally. Waterford said analysis by the think tank, which has been benchmarking Sydney against other international cities for the past decade, had consistently noticed a disconnect between Sydney’s daily life and the way the city was perceived internationally. The critical missing factor? Its people.



The ubiquitous images of Sydney’s built landmarks and coastline ignored the way in which most of the city’s 5.5 million residents enjoyed and celebrated the city, at events such as the Sydney Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras parade down Oxford Street and the Ramadan Nights festival in Lakemba. Thousands of Sydneysiders attend the yearly Ramadan Nights festival in Lakemba. Wolter Peeters “The people of Sydney are interesting, and really attractive to the world; they are exciting to global investors, to visitors who are looking for rich cultural experiences, to students who are wondering where they should go to university – Sydney’s got it all,” Waterford said. “But we don’t sell that human story.” The report said Sydney was typically viewed positively on an international level when it came to reputation, governance and liveability. Areas such as business dynamism, innovation intensity and cultural influence were “where Sydney’s underlying performance is strongest but under-recognised”.



Waterford said the research showed that this disconnect was costing the city $3.3 billion every year due to global investors, start-ups, major firms and conference organisers choosing other cities. Mardi Gras is one of Sydney’s biggest celebrations. Flavio Brancaleone “It’s also made up of visitors who come once, see those amazing icons and never return, rather than coming back time and time again because they can never get to the bottom of how great this city is,” he said. Waterford said the solution was “not a marketing campaign or a new logo”. “It’s about everybody recognising there are great things that Sydney has going for it, and then including them in the stories they’re sharing with the world,” he said.



Related Article City life Win for golfers as final Moore Park plans are revealed The next phase of the Sydney Global campaign involved building “a coalition of storytellers”, from everyday Sydneysiders to international sports and music stars, he said. They would then develop a “cheat sheet” or “brand bible” outlining the city’s key assets, with a view to telling a more comprehensive story about the city and boosting Sydney’s international presence. “It will be about [identifying], these are the things that make Sydney great, now let’s all go and tell the world those things,” Waterford said.
